strengths: The paper is well-motivated, grounding its computational architecture in established cognitive neuroscience theories of predictive coding during natural language comprehension.

The preliminary verification experiment effectively motivates the architectural design, empirically validating both the predictive distance (peaking around d=4) and the selection of six language-related regions of interest (ROIs).

The experimental design follows sound splitting practices (adopting the contamination-free cross-subject split from Yin et al., 2023) and includes comprehensive analyses, such as ROI ablations, predictive distance effects, and positional error analysis within repetition time (TR) frames.
PREDFT consistently outperforms the primary state-of-the-art baseline (UniCoRN) across different sequence lengths on standard n-gram overlap metrics.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons are limited almost exclusively to UniCoRN. Even if other recent works (e.g., Tang et al., 2023; Ye et al., 2023) used different splits or per-subject evaluations, re-implementing or adapting standard neural sequence-to-sequence baselines would make the comparative evaluation more convincing.

Evaluation relies solely on lexical overlap metrics (BLEU, ROUGE). In open-vocabulary brain decoding, semantic similarity metrics (such as BERTScore, Sentence-BERT embedding similarity, or pairwise semantic ranking accuracy) are standard and crucial, especially when lexical match is sparse and BLEU-3/4 scores remain very low.
No statistical significance testing is reported for the performance gains over UniCoRN across test subjects or narrative stories.

strengths: Principled integration of neuroscience theory: The paper elegantly bridges cognitive predictive coding theory with neural decoding architecture, moving beyond purely black-box empirical approaches.

Methodological rigor: The authors first empirically verify the predictive coding capacity in fMRI data and determine optimal prediction distance and relevant ROIs before designing the dual-network PREDFT architecture.

Attention to experimental validity: The authors adopt the strict non-overlapping cross-subject split from Yin et al. (2023) to avoid data leakage issues that have affected prior literature in this task.

Insightful analysis: The positional decoding error analysis (Appendix B) provides an insightful explanation of information loss caused by fMRI repetition time (TR) and how predictive coding representations help alleviate it.
weaknesses: Limited baseline comparisons: The empirical comparison is essentially restricted to UniCoRN. While justifications are provided for omitting other recent methods, adapting or re-implementing additional competitive baselines under the same clean evaluation protocol would make the empirical claims substantially stronger.

Evaluation metrics: Brain decoding is notoriously prone to producing semantically related paraphrases that do not have exact n-gram overlap. The evaluation relies solely on surface-level n-gram overlap metrics (BLEU, ROUGE) and lacks semantic similarity evaluations (e.g., BERTScore, text-embedding cosine similarity, or pairwise classification/ranking accuracy commonly used in the literature).

Absolute generation quality and interpretability: As evident from Table 3, the reconstructed language is still fragmented and grammatically degraded. A deeper human evaluation or fine-grained semantic evaluation would clarify whether the model reconstructs true communicative intent or mainly opportunistic word associations.

strengths: Novel and principled motivation: The paper thoughtfully bridges predictive coding theory in cognitive neuroscience with the technical architecture of fMRI-to-text decoding, moving beyond naive end-to-end mapping.

Methodological care regarding data splits: The authors explicitly address and avoid the data leakage issues prevalent in prior cross-subject fMRI decoding studies by following the rigorous split protocol established by Yin et al. (2023).

Comprehensive empirical analyses and ablations: The manuscript provides insightful diagnostic analyses, including region-of-interest (ROI) ablation (BPC vs. random vs. whole cortex), prediction distance variations, and temporal error distribution across fMRI repetition times (TR).
weaknesses: Reliance solely on surface n-gram overlap metrics: The evaluation is restricted to BLEU and ROUGE. Given the notorious difficulty of exact-match n-gram recovery from noisy BOLD signals and the high degree of paraphrasing in language generation, semantic similarity metrics (such as BERTScore, BLEURT, or sentence embedding cosine similarity) and fluency/perplexity evaluations are critical to gauge whether the semantic content is genuinely reconstructed.

Limited baseline comparisons: The empirical comparison is essentially restricted to a single baseline, UniCoRN. While the authors justify why certain prior models (Tang et al., 2023; Ye et al., 2023) could not be directly reused due to differing splits/preprocessing, implementing a standard competitive pre-trained sequence-to-sequence baseline (e.g., a standard BART or LLaMA-based decoder with fMRI prefix without predictive coding) would have provided a much clearer benchmark of progress.

Quality of generated text remains largely degenerated: As seen in the qualitative examples (Table 3), the decoded outputs often suffer from repetitive tokens and ungrammatical phrasing (e.g., 'and and and he and of under the next'). A deeper discussion of repetition degeneration, decoding strategies (e.g., beam search vs. nucleus sampling), and grammar quality is needed.

strengths: Strong cognitive and neuroscientific grounding: The paper leverages predictive coding theory to motivate the integration of future-word prediction representations from specific brain regions into fMRI-to-text decoding.

Well-designed architecture: The dual-network design (main decoding network + auxiliary side network) enables the side encoder to learn predictive representations using future tokens during training, while requiring only fMRI/ROI inputs during inference.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The authors validate the method on two widely recognized naturalistic language fMRI datasets (LeBel's and Narratives) across both within-subject and cross-subject evaluation protocols, achieving competitive or superior performance compared to strong existing baselines.

In-depth analysis: The paper features thorough exploratory analyses, including ROI selection (BPC vs. Whole cortex vs. Random), systematic sweeps over prediction distance $d$ and length $l$, decoding error distributions across TR intervals, and chance-level sanity checks.
weaknesses: Limitations in reconstruction fluency and higher-order n-grams: While BLEU-1 and ROUGE1-F show notable improvements, higher-order n-gram metrics (BLEU-3 and BLEU-4) remain very low across all models (often below 2%), and qualitative samples in Table 8 demonstrate that generated texts still suffer from significant disfluency and repetition.

Sensitivity to predictive hyperparameters: Decoding performance depends heavily on the choices of prediction distance $d$ and length $l$. The optimal settings appear to require extensive parameter searches and may vary depending on the scanner's repetition time (TR) and linguistic stimulus presentation rate.

Baseline comparability: The compared baselines utilize distinct architectures and pretrained language models (e.g., BART in UniCoRN, LLaMA-2 in BrainLLM, GPT-2 in Tang et al.), making it somewhat difficult to strictly isolate architectural gains versus language model capacity differences, although the internal ablation (PREDFT w/o SideNet) helps address this.

strengths: Grounding fMRI-to-text decoding in the neuroscientific theory of predictive coding is conceptually well-motivated and provides a fresh perspective on neural language decoding architectures.

The experimental setup is rigorous, carefully avoiding known data leakage issues in cross-subject evaluation on the Narratives dataset and testing on both within-subject (LeBel) and cross-subject benchmarks.

Comprehensive empirical analyses are provided, including systematic exploration of prediction distance and length, comparison of ROI selections (predictive ROIs vs. whole brain vs. random), ablation studies, and an insightful positional error analysis regarding fMRI temporal resolution (information loss slope).
weaknesses: Mechanistic attribution remains somewhat ambiguous: it is not entirely disentangled whether the performance gains stem from genuine brain predictive representations captured in the selected ROIs or simply from the auxiliary multi-task objective (predicting future text sequences as a regularizer during training).

Generated language quality remains limited in fluency and coherence (as visible in the qualitative samples in Table 8), with higher-order n-gram metrics (BLEU-3/4) remaining very low across all systems.

The temporal alignment mechanism between variable-rate text tokens and fixed-interval fMRI frames (and the exact attention masking logic in the predictive coding cross-attention) could be formalized and described with greater mathematical precision.

strengths: Principled integration of cognitive neuroscience: The paper grounds its design in predictive coding theory, thoughtfully utilizing prior neuroscientific findings to motivate a dual-stream architecture (main decoding network + side predictive network).

Thorough preliminary verification: The authors systematically verify predictive coding dynamics (optimal prediction distance and length) and region-of-interest (ROI) responsiveness before designing the decoding architecture.

Methodological rigor regarding evaluation leakage: For cross-subject evaluation on the Narratives dataset, the authors properly adopt data-splitting protocols that avoid subject and stimulus leakage (addressing flaws identified in earlier literature).

Comprehensive empirical analyses: The paper provides extensive experiments across both within-subject (LeBel) and cross-subject (Narratives) setups, thorough ablations (side network removal, ROI parcellation variations, chance-level controls), parameter sensitivity sweeps ($l, d, \lambda$), and an insightful positional error analysis across fMRI repetition times (TR).
weaknesses: Generation quality and low higher-order overlap: While PREDFT achieves gains on BLEU-1 and ROUGE-1, higher-order n-gram metrics remain very low (BLEU-3 and BLEU-4 are consistently below 2–5%), and qualitative examples (Table 8) show substantial disfluency and degenerate token repetitions.

Confound between neural predictive coding and hemodynamic response latency: Because the BOLD response peaks with a 4–6 second hemodynamic delay, it is difficult to conclusively disentangle whether the side network captures genuine neural forward predictions or simply exploits delayed vascular responses to words presented subsequent to the current frame.

Backbone heterogeneity and metric trade-offs: Baseline models employ disparate pre-trained backbones (e.g., LLaMA-2 in BrainLLM, BART in UniCoRN, GPT in Tang et al.), whereas PREDFT is trained largely from scratch. Notably, BrainLLM maintains a higher BERTScore across all three subjects in Table 1, indicating that PREDFT's improvements are largely concentrated in lexical overlap rather than semantic representation.

Absence of standard semantic-level retrieval/identification metrics: Prior literature in fMRI decoding (e.g., Tang et al., 2023) heavily relies on rank-based candidate identification accuracy and semantic embedding cosine similarity. Relying exclusively on surface-level n-gram overlap (BLEU/ROUGE) underemphasizes semantic gist reconstruction.
